papers.title: What message features influence the intention to share misinformation about COVID-19 on social media? The role of efficacy and novelty
papers.finding: Korean experiment (N=1,012) on how novelty and efficacy of misinformation affect sharing through emotion and credibility.

papers.title: Who spread COVID-19 (mis)information online? Differential informedness, psychological mechanisms, and intervention strategies
papers.finding: Chinese surveys: misinformed and uninformed people were more likely to spread misinformation; positive-emotion content spread more.

papers.why: Supports teaching students to seek news actively rather than rely on feeds or AI summaries.
papers.title: Social media may hinder learning about science; social media's role in learning about COVID-19
papers.finding: US two-wave panel. Getting news from social media fostered a news-finds-me belief, which left people less informed and more misinformed about COVID-19.

children.name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
children.blurb: Coaching students through primary sources means using a school configured AI tool to ask the kinds of questions a historian would ask while students read letters, speeches, photographs, and government records.

children.name: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
children.blurb: Historical role play, labeled as simulation, lets students interview or question a program that imagines a historical figure, a delegate at a constitutional convention, or a witness to an event.

children.name: Perspectives and Missing Voices
children.blurb: Perspectives and Missing Voices is a social studies use of AI in which a tool helps students compare how different people might describe the same event and helps teachers find groups that textbooks often leave out.

children.name: Why a Teacher Reads First
children.blurb: Every AI tool that produces perspectives, summaries, or historical content should be read by a teacher before students see it.

children.name: Current Events and Misinformation
children.blurb: The idea of current events and misinformation is about using AI to help prepare leveled news discussions while teaching students to verify what they see.

children.name: Civic Simulations, Debate, and Mock Trial
children.blurb: Civic simulations, debate, and mock trial let students practice civics rather than only read about it.

children.name: Timelines, Maps, and Local History
children.blurb: This idea uses visual tools like timelines and maps, plus local history interviews, to help students understand sequence, place, and community.

children.name: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
children.blurb: This idea is that AI can add world language practice when human practice partners are scarce, while teachers keep judgment over feedback and grades.

children.name: Translation as a Lesson
children.blurb: Translation as a Lesson is a translation critique exercise in which students translate a passage themselves and then compare their version with one from Microsoft Translator, identifying where the machine got the meaning right, where it lost tone or idiom, and where it made outright errors.

children.name: Access for Every Student
children.blurb: Access for Every Student means using AI to make social studies, civics, and world languages content readable and understandable for all learners without lowering the intellectual demand.

children.name: Heritage Speakers and Family Languages
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI to support students who speak a language other than English at home, especially when their speaking and listening are stronger than their reading and writing.

children.name: Geography and Data
children.blurb: Geography and data can be combined in social studies so students examine population, climate, or trade information for regions and identify patterns.

children.name: Planning and Assessment in These Subjects
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI to draft planning and assessment materials in social studies, civics, and world languages, then having the teacher review and edit them.

sections.body: Social studies, civics, and world languages are the part of school life where students study people, events, choices, and languages, and the book says AI can answer questions in the voice of a historical figure, show how different people might see the same event, give a language learner endless conversation practice, and let a class explore economic or political choices through simulation. The book also says these tools produce fluent text that can include invented quotes, dates, and sources, and in history and civics an invented quote attributed to a real person can distort the past and mislead students about what people actually believed. The chapter covers primary source coaching, historical role play, perspective taking and missing voices, current events and misinformation, civic simulations and debate, timelines and local history, and several uses in world languages. A section on bias explains why every perspective tool needs a teacher reading first, and Figure 9.2 maps the ideas and their evidence. Only one idea here carries strong evidence, so most should begin as small pilots.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that what works is a simple review practice teachers actually follow, where any AI generated historical content, perspective, or source is read by the teacher before students use it, simulations are labeled, and quotes are verified against real sources. A general policy on AI use is not enough on its own, because what counts is a routine that teachers apply lesson by lesson. What does not work is the convincing simulation, where a class interviews a simulated historical figure, students copy memorable quotes into essays, nobody checks whether the figure ever said them, and the invented history spreads after the essays are graded. The rule the book holds to is the board question about trust in what students learn, asking who checks AI produced historical content, perspectives, or translations before students rely on them. The Thirty Day Move is to adopt the simulation rules in Figure 9.3 and the teacher check in Figure 9.4 for every social studies and world language class, share them in a short meeting with an example of an invented quote, and run one misinformation lab in at least one grade using Figure 9.5.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: For a teacher starting with sources, Coaching Students Through Primary Sources and Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation show how to use real documents and keep role play clearly marked, while Perspectives and Missing Voices extends that work to whose viewpoint is included and whose is left out. Why a Teacher Reads First is the hinge for all of these, and Current Events and Misinformation is where the research this site holds fits, including What message features influence the intention to share misinformation about COVID-19 on social media? The role of efficacy and novelty, Who spread COVID-19 (mis)information online? Differential informedness, psychological mechanisms, and intervention strategies, and Social media may hinder learning about science; social media's role in learning about COVID-19. Civic Simulations, Debate, and Mock Trial and Timelines, Maps, and Local History carry the same checking habit into civic practice and into time and place, while World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment and Translation as a Lesson show where AI gives practice and where human judgment must stay. Access for Every Student, Heritage Speakers and Family Languages, and Geography and Data widen the map to who is in the room, what languages they bring, and how data and place are read. Planning and Assessment in These Subjects is where a leader or teacher turns the chapter into lessons and checks, and a parent can use the same pages to ask what was verified before it reached their child.
